title: Boniface and the oak
hook: an English monk to the Germans, remembered for felling a sacred oak and dying a martyr

segments.voice: Yesterday, the triumph of Orthodoxy, and your line was windows restored: icons carried home. What did you look through on purpose? Day eight hundred three.

An axe bites into an enormous oak in a clearing in Hesse, in what is now Germany. The tree is sacred to the people who live here. The account calls it the oak of Jupiter, giving their god a Roman name. A crowd has gathered, and the crowd is cursing the man with the axe. He's a monk from England named Boniface, and the local Christians have urged him on. He makes one cut. Then, says the account, a great wind from above shakes the tree, and it comes crashing down. Today's word is that monk and that tree.

Our main source is a life of Boniface written by a priest named Willibald. Boniface was born in England, became a monk, and left a settled life to preach among the Germanic peoples across the sea. The oak is the scene his story turns on. In Willibald's telling, the people who had cursed him saw the tree fall and began to praise God instead. And Boniface used the timber to build a small chapel, dedicated to Saint Peter. The wood of the old shrine became the walls of the new one. Now the honest part. It was someone's holy tree. The people who gathered in that clearing weren't villains in their own story. And Christians have disagreed about how to meet another people's sacred places. Earlier on this path, Pope Gregory advised the missionaries in England to keep the old temples and take out only the idols: bless, don't destroy. Boniface's story goes the other way. Both are part of the church's story, and both are remembered. Then the ending. As an old man, Boniface went to preach in Frisia, near the North Sea. At dawn one morning his camp was attacked. Willibald says his companions reached for weapons, and Boniface stopped them. Scripture, he told them, teaches us not to repay evil for evil. In the King James words of Paul to the Romans: "Recompense to no man evil for evil." He was killed there with his companions. Tradition adds that he held up a book of the gospels over his head as the blow fell. So the man remembered for an axe died refusing a sword. Christians honor him as a martyr and as an apostle to the Germans.
screen: `A MONK FROM ENGLAND, ACROSS THE SEA.`
then, large: `RECOMPENSE TO NO MAN EVIL FOR EVIL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one thing you need to stop worshiping. Not someone else's. Yours. Settle, and breathe. Christians reserve worship for God. But anything can quietly take that place: a phone, a number in a bank account, someone's approval, being right, being busy. Ask yourself, without hurry, what has grown too big. Don't fix it yet. Just name it, honestly, in a word. If you pray, you can hand that word to God and ask for help cutting it down to size. If you don't, simply hold the word, and notice how much room it takes up. The bell holds the time.
Boniface and the oak. The English monk who felled a sacred tree in Germany and built a chapel from its wood, and who died refusing to fight back.

howItsDone: Boniface is honored as a saint and martyr, especially in Germany and the Netherlands; Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches remember him on his feast day, and his tomb is kept at Fulda.

notes: Willibald, Life of Boniface 6: the oak of Jupiter at Geismar, felled with the counsel of converts, a wind from above, the cursing pagans praising God, an oratory to St Peter from the timber. Paraphrased; the split into four parts is left out. Confirm chapter numbers.
Willibald, Life 8: martyrdom in Frisia at dawn; Boniface forbids resistance, citing scripture not to render evil for evil. Paraphrased; confirm.
'Not long after his death' for Willibald's life: confirm (usually dated within about a decade).
The gospel book raised over his head (the Ragyndrudis codex at Fulda) is attributed to tradition. Confirm.
'As an old man' is in Willibald; confirm.

Reference to day 790 (Gregory's letter to Mellitus, Bede 1.30): 'keep the old temples and take out only the idols'. Confirm framing and that it is fair to both approaches and to pre-Christian Germanic religion.
'The Roman name for their thunder god' (Donar/Thor) is an interpretive gloss on Willibald's 'Jupiter'; confirm or cut.
